title: Habitat for Humanity highlights Nepal's growing housing crisis - KEYE
description: Habitat for Humanity highlights Nepal's growing housing crisis  KEYE
publisher.title: KEYE
full_article:
A safe place to call home is something every family deserves. But for communities across Nepal, finding secure and affordable housing has become an increasingly difficult challenge, made even more urgent by devastating flash floods and extreme weather.

New global research from Habitat for Humanity reveals the enormous pressure families in Nepal were already facing before the recent disaster.

Eliza Sthapit, National Director of Habitat for Humanity Nepal, joined We Are Austin to discuss the findings, the challenges facing families and why building stronger, more resilient homes is critical for the future.

Watch the full video above to learn more about Habitat for Humanity's work in Nepal!

Housing is a major source of stress for families

According to Habitat for Humanity's global research, 68% of people surveyed in Nepal identified housing as one of the biggest sources of stress in their lives.

That's nearly double the 35% reported across the countries surveyed.

The findings highlight how deeply housing concerns affect families, even before natural disasters place additional pressure on communities.

For many households, the struggle to find safe, stable housing is about much more than having a roof overhead. It can affect financial security, health and a family's ability to plan for the future.

Extreme weather adds to an existing crisis

Recent flash floods across Nepal have brought renewed attention to the importance of safe housing and disaster preparedness.

For families already facing housing insecurity, severe weather can create additional challenges, including damage to homes, displacement and the difficult process of rebuilding.

As communities work toward recovery, Habitat for Humanity is emphasizing the need for housing solutions that address both immediate needs and future risks.

What is resilient housing?

Building a home is one thing. Building a home that can better withstand future disasters is another.

Resilient housing refers to homes designed, constructed or improved to better withstand environmental hazards, including flooding, severe storms and other climate-related threats.

The goal is not simply to rebuild after a disaster, but to help families and communities become better prepared for the next one.

For Nepal, where challenging terrain and extreme weather can increase risks, resilient housing is an important part of long-term community stability.

A global challenge with local impact

While Nepal faces its own unique housing challenges, Habitat for Humanity's research highlights a larger issue affecting families around the world.

Housing affordability, safety and stability are concerns that extend across borders, including here in the United States.

By examining how families experience housing stress in different countries, the research helps bring greater attention to the human impact of the global housing crisis.

How you can help

Habitat for Humanity continues working with communities around the world to expand access to safe, affordable housing and support long-term resilience.

Through community partnerships, housing initiatives and disaster recovery efforts, the organization aims to help more families build a stable foundation for the future.

To explore the research, learn more about Habitat for Humanity's work or find ways to get involved, visit Habitat.org.

title: China cites non-existent Tibetan refugee threats to refuse reopening Nepal border trade post - Tibetan Review
description: China cites non-existent Tibetan refugee threats to refuse reopening Nepal border trade post  Tibetan Review
publisher.title: Tibetan Review
full_article:
(TibetanReview.net, Oct19’26) – The Tatopani crossing in Sindhupalchok is the most viable route for Nepal to conduct border trade with China through Tibet. However, despite intensified diplomatic efforts from Kathmandu, China remains unwilling to reopen it for regular border exchanges due mainly to its security concerns related to unsubstantiated allegations of Tibetan refugee movements and activities.

The border point has been opened only temporarily, for just three days, to facilitate the import of goods for the Dashain festival, reported english.nepalnews.com Oct 18. The festival is Nepal’s longest, grandest, and most important, and lasts 15 days and began on Oct 11 this year. It is celebrated to honour Goddess Durga and her victory over the demon Mahishasura.

Nepal intensified its diplomatic efforts to reopen the Tatopani border crossing with China after floods and landslides disrupted alternative trade routes, but Beijing has yet to commit to restoring regular operations, citing security concerns, logistical difficulties and recurring landslides, reported kathmandupost.com Oct 17.

The report cited Nepali officials familiar with border security as saying Chinese concerns about Tibetan refugees entering Nepal and possible anti-China activities along the frontier had also complicated efforts to resume trade through the Tatopani crossing.

Reopening the Tatopani crossing has become more urgent since the Aug 26 Bhotekoshi flood closed the Rasuwa­gadhi border point, Nepal’s major trade route with China through Tibet. But China is only offering assistance to restore Rasuwa­gadhi as the main trading point, although even this is bound to take a long time.

The Tatopani crossing in Sindhupalchok, Nepal.

The Korala border crossing in Mustang, another alternative, also remains disrupted by floods and landslides, leaving goods ordered by traders stranded ahead of Dashain, Nepal’s most widely celebrated festival and the biggest shopping season of the year, the report said.

At a meeting on Oct 14 with Nepal’s Industry, Commerce and Supplies Minister Deepak Kumar Sah, Chinese Ambassador Zhang Maoming indicated that Tatopani could be reopened for a short period to meet festival demand, but that its long-term operation would require a detailed assessment. The ambassador has mainly cited security challenges, while also referring to logistical problems and frequent landslides as additional complications.

Beijing’s wider concerns was stated to be its allegations of cross-border movement of Tibetan refugees along the Nepal-Tibet border.

The report noted that during the government led by the Nepal Communist Party, formed through the merger of the CPN-UML and the Maoists, the home ministry decided to stop deporting Tibetan refugees to India. It bears noting that this was a result of international pressure, especially from the United sates. It cited a former senior administrator who served as chief district officer in Sindhupalchok as saying Chinese officials continued to provide information about people crossing from Tibet, and Nepali authorities acted on some of those reports.

A former chief district officer in Sindhupalchok has recalled Chinese officials expressing concern over the alleged growing presence of followers of the Dalai Lama in border areas. However, investigations by Nepal Police and the National Investigation Department did not establish the scale of activity claimed by the Chinese side, the report noted.

“There may be people using the area as a transit point, but we did not find the kind of followers they described,” the former official has said, adding that subsequent administrative action had made such activity less likely.

Another former additional chief research director of the National Investigation Department has said the number of young Tibetans leaving their homes and coming to Nepal had declined as China had developed Tibet and sought to relocate settlements further inland, away from the border.

The report said that a few years ago, China had proposed forming a joint monitoring team with Nepal, comprising officials from the administration in Tibet and their counterparts in Sindhupalchok.

“The proposal was put forward as a way to coordinate responses to disasters and other issues, and it reached the home secretary through the relevant channel. The district security committee also endorsed it and forwarded it. But ultimately, the ministry didn’t approve it,” the report quoted the official as saying.

The report said that despite these concerns, officials and traders say the crossing’s economic importance warrants a fresh effort to reach an understanding with Beijing.

Tatopani was closed following the 2015 earthquake and reopened for limited cargo movement in May 2019. It was again closed during the Covid pandemic in 2020. Imports remained restricted largely to selected goods, while exports have struggled to resume meaningfully despite China permitting outbound trade in 2023. Before the earthquake, Nepal exported copper utensils, handicrafts, flour, noodles, eggs, vegetable ghee and medicinal herbs through the crossing, the report said.

The Araniko Highway, built in the 1960s, was stated to be Nepal’s principal road link with China through before the Rasuwa­gadhi-Kerung route opened in 2014. Repeated closures have since weakened Tatopani’s role, the report said.

title: Long Island families left with uncertainty after Nepal ends flood rescue - Newsday
description: Long Island families left with uncertainty after Nepal ends flood rescue  Newsday
publisher.title: Newsday
full_article:
Nearly two months after flash floods swept through the Nepal-China border region, Rajendra Karki, of Hicksville, is still holding onto hope his sister Krishna Kumari Shrestha, 62, is somewhere out there.

Though Nepalese officials told Karki's family his sister likely hadn’t survived the flood, he still was upset to hear search and rescue efforts have ceased.

"We hope they magically find our sister. ... I wish they’d continue searching for people. We don’t know if my sister died. We’re all hoping they’re alive," said Karki, 48, who told Newsday Krishna was at home with three relatives — Dhan Kumari Shrestha, 64; Deb Kumari Shrestha, 59; Kopila Shreatha, 36 — when the flood inundated the Himalayan region.

A September report from World Weather Attribution said the Aug. 26 disaster was caused by a rock-ice avalanche that evolved into a debris flood. The nonprofit found human-caused warming that melted glaciers and thawed frozen ground likely further destabilized an already vulnerable mountain slope.

Last week, the office of Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah announced it concluded search and rescue operations for victims of the floods, The Associated Press reported. The bodies of at least 1,455 people have been recovered, but 5,285 remain missing.

Rajendra Karki of Hicksville and his sister Krishna Kumari Shrestha photographed in 2006. Credit: Family photo

The president of the Long Island Nepalese Society, Sabitra Siwakoti, said the decision to halt the search and rescue effort has generated mixed emotions within her group. Some believe the Nepalese government did everything it could, while others wish search efforts would continue a bit longer.

"Even one body is a big deal for us. That’s a human being. But unfortunately, this disaster [came without] any warning," Siwakoti said. "Personally, I feel like they try their best. ... The Nepali government spent a lot of money and lots of resources to search for them as far as we know."

Siwakoti said many members of the group wanted to fly to Nepal to support their families but concluded that money was better spent contributing to the Nepalese government’s search efforts and financially supporting displaced relatives.

"I tried to go right away, but my parents said, ‘It’s too fresh, and even if you come here, you cannot do anything right now. You'd just be crying. That's what we're doing here,’ " said Karki, who watched from afar as his family priest cremated bodies made of kusha grass to represent his four missing relatives in a Hindu ceremony, called Pratika Antyeshti.

With recent developments, he hopes to return as soon as possible to help memorialize his sister, who was a retired school teacher.

Just days before the floods, Karki said his sister sent him a message wishing him blessings for the Hindu festival Rakhi, which celebrates the bond between brothers and sisters.

He hadn’t initially panicked after being unable to contact her after the disaster. But when her husband and two sons called days later, Karki knew something was wrong.

"They were crying and that’s when I knew the news. ... I could not believe that. It’s not possible. Her home is not close to the river. I said, ‘How could the flood go that high?’," he said.

Newsday also followed up with Aditi Patel, who said in September her mother, Tejal Vyomesh Patel, her mother-in-law, Amita Amin and family friend Jitendra Manubhai Patel had crossed the border into Tibet with a tour group at the time of the catastrophic floods. About 400 family members and friends of the tour group gathered in Queens on Sept. 27 for a prayer meeting.

Unanswered questions

Amita Amin, 67, of Roslyn Heights, left, and Tejal Vyomesh Patel, 64, of New Jersey, went missing after the deadly floods. Credit: Nepal Trekking Planner

Patel, 42, of Old Westbury, said she received death certificates for her mother and mother-in-law from the Nepalese government on Friday morning, which she obtained via email from the United States government.

"It was not easy seeing that in the email," Patel said. "It was kind of like this is the end of the road."

She did not receive one for their friend.

While the documents provide some closure, Patel said some questions are left unanswered. "Mentally, our closure would be knowing exactly where they were."

Patel and her father-in-law traveled to Nepal in September and met with the owner of the tour group company, whose own son-in-law and guide on the trip are missing. They also took a helicopter ride with the Nepalese army.

"You think you see it just like in videos and you think you know it, and then seeing it in person, it just hits you 20 times harder," Patel said. "There is no way anybody would have made it out alive if they were within that disaster zone."

Seeing the full scope of the disaster also gave them perspective on just how many people it affected, as the mudslides wiped out "countless other lives, houses, businesses," as well as entire families.

"It just seemed not so just personal to us anymore. It just seemed like such a big humanitarian crisis. ... There are thousands of other people like us," Patel said.

Patel said recent identifications of 9/11 victims gave her hope that someday, her loved ones' DNA could be confirmed through collection of samples.

But right now, Patel said the hardest thing about this is someday explaining it all to her children, who are too young to understand.

"They ask about them, they talk about them and it doesn't make it easier for us," Patel said. "This seems unfair that they have to be without both their grandmothers."

Kathmandu, October 20

Mahanawami, the ninth day of the Bada Dashain festival, is being observed across Nepal today with special worship of Goddess Durga Bhawani and offerings at temples and homes.

Observed on the ninth day of the waxing moon in the lunar month of Asoj, Mahanawami is marked by prayers, rituals and offerings to the goddess. Jamara, the sacred barley shoots grown during Dashain, are also offered at various shrines.

Animal sacrifices, including male goats, ducks, roosters and buffaloes, are performed at temples dedicated to the goddess. Those who do not follow the tradition of animal sacrifice offer fruits and vegetables instead.

Devotees also recite religious scriptures, including the Durga Saptasati and Devi Stotra, at homes and temples.

According to the Markandeya Purana, Goddess Chamunda killed the demon Raktabij on Mahanawami. The day is therefore marked by special worship of the goddess, including animal sacrifices in communities that observe the tradition.

Security forces also perform Kot Puja , a ritual worship of their armouries, on this occasion.

In Kathmandu, the Taleju Temple at Hanumandhoka is opened to the public for devotees to pay homage to Goddess Tulaja Bhawani. The temple is open to the public only on Mahanawami.

Members of the Newar community also worship Bhimsen, a Hindu deity, on the occasion, with animal sacrifices performed by those who follow the tradition.

title: Nepal secures victory by 10 runs against Oman - The Rising Nepal

Kathmandu, Oct 20: Nepal achieved a 10-run victory against Oman in the ICC Cricket World Cup League-2 competition, marking the nation's third triumph in the series.

Having won the coin toss and elected to bat first at the Al Amerat Cricket Ground (Ministry Turf 1) in Oman, Nepal established a target of 281 runs.

Oman's batting effort resulted in 270 runs with the loss of seven wickets across the full 50 overs. Jatinder Singh and Hamad Mirza each contributed half-centuries for Oman, accumulating 89 and 87 runs respectively.

Hasnain Shah concluded with an unbeaten 40 runs. Additionally, Hasnain ul Wahab contributed 15 runs, and captain Binayak Shukla added 13 runs.

For Nepal's bowling performance, Dipendra Singh Airee and Lalit Rajvanshi each claimed two wickets, while captain Sandeep Lamichhane and Nandan Yadav secured one wicket apiece.

Nepal's batting lineup featured three half-century contributors. Rohit Kumar Poudel scored 80 runs from 81 deliveries, including two boundaries and two sixes, while Dipendra Singh Airee accumulated 69 runs from 62 balls with four sixes and three boundaries.

Dev Khanal scored 57 runs from 65 balls, featuring four boundaries and one six. Ishaan Pandey contributed 29 runs, and Basir Ahmed added 17 runs. Shah Faisal took five wickets for Oman.

Following this victory, Nepal advanced to sixth position in the standings. Nepal has won 14 of 36 matches in the current League-2 edition, drawn 20 matches, and lost 2 matches, accumulating 30 points from 36 games.(RSS)

title: Everything you need to know about Newar rituals - Nepali Times
description: Everything you need to know about Newar rituals  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Who would have thought that votive offerings, sacrifices and feasts would be the subject of a sociological study? But that is exactly what German heritage conservationist and architect Niels Gutschow has done in his new book.

Gifts Offerings Sacrifices: The Art and Practice of Ritual Offerings of the Newars in Nepal is a detailed but clinical documentation of rituals that expounds on their cultural and religious significance.

The book starts by defining the terms ‘gift’, ‘offering’ and ‘sacrifice’, and how they differ. A gift is given voluntarily, without a payment in return. An offering is a form of worship. Sacrifice which we now associate with animal sacrifice in the context of festivals and rituals originally meant to make something holy.

There is also the term ‘दान’, a donation given to those in distress without expecting anything in return. I have a quibble here: is it really selfless when the very act of dana is to cultivate punya, merit? How about donations for disaster survivors, where the donor posts pictures offering a cheque to the Finance Minister? Can corporate social responsibility be considered a दान?

In his foreword, Gutschow notes that the details in the book are based on ‘repeated observations or even participation’, and should not be taken as the be all and end all about Newar offerings and sacrifices

Rituals which involve purifying families polluted by death for example used to be an obligation, but are now shunned by parapriests or purity specialists. There is a larger socio-political context behind this denial rooted in casteism and untouchability, we learn.

Gutschow first came to Nepal in 1962, and returned almost annually to work on heritage conservation projects, including the restoration of Purajimath in Bhaktapur. He lived there till 2021, observing and participating in rituals.

The introduction has an elaborate list of the ingredients in Newar offerings that include edibles, liquids, unhusked rice, tashi or citron which signifies both fertility and longevity, betel nuts which feature prominently in many important life rituals in Newar culture, spices, sweets, buffalo meat, and more. This is all intangible heritage.

The book is divided into three parts – urban rituals, life cycle rituals and domestic rituals. Urban rituals include the 9-9 Biska chariot festival, Yenyapunhi, Indra Jatra and Saparu in Kathmandu.

The Dasain chapter should have a trigger alert for images of ritual sacrifices, as well as their religious justification. An entire chapter is dedicated to Buddhist rituals, which in contrast, renounce animal sacrifice.

Life cycle rituals include Annaprasana first rice feeding, the Ihi initiation for girls, Kyatapuja for boys, the Barha seclusion of the maiden, and finally, Ihipa marriage. There is a lot Newars like me did not know about the socio-cultural significance of many of these practices

But perhaps the book's most fascinating part is the explanation for why the betel nut is so essential. A plant native to the Philippines is indispensible in Newar life and death rituals. ‘The bride dissociates herself from her natal home by offering ten betel nuts and a pouch with five betel nuts to her parents, to relatives, and symbolically even to those absent.’

‘...Three days after the marriage the matchmaker hands five betel nuts to the newly wed husband, for him to pass to all members of his wife’s family to confirm his obligations as a wife-taker.’

Obligations as a wife-take means supporting his wife’s family in case of death, the wife is obliged to act as the unpolluted daughter and perform subsequent death rituals.

There is also a short chapter on the rare celebration of someone reaching 100 years. Gutschow attends the centenary ceremony of Chalmaya Shakya in Bhaktapur where ‘she enters a large, painted water pot, marked with a triangle and a dot in the centre. The pot represents a source of all reality, the divine or cosmic womb from which everything is born. Leaving the receptacle or womb stands for the celebrant’s ritual rebirth, which implies a prior ritual death.’

Swonti, Tihar and Yomaripunhi are also featured as well as significances of second and fourth birthdays. A person who is celebrating their birthday should stay home on that day to avoid ‘unfortunate occurrences, such as crossing a body of water’. That was new to me.

Other tomes go into much more detail about Newar festivals, but this is a compact and exquisitely produced book that tells you everything you were never told about why we have all those gifts, offerings and sacrifices in our community.

Gifts Offerings Sacrifices: The Art and Practice of Ritual Offerings of the Newars in Nepal

Seen by Neils Gutschow

title: Nepal to lower water levels in 4 glacial lakes: Move to reduce India’s flood risk, prevent disasters like A... - Bhaskar English
description: Nepal to lower water levels in 4 glacial lakes: Move to reduce India’s flood risk, prevent disasters like A...  Bhaskar English
publisher.title: Bhaskar English
full_article:
English News

International

Nepal Glacial Lakes Flood Risk Mitigation Project | India Safety Measures

Nepal to lower water levels in 4 glacial lakes: Move to reduce India’s flood risk, prevent disasters like August’s Bhotekoshi floods

Kathmandu 34 minutes ago



Copy link

Nepal has launched a plan to reduce the risk of devastating floods by lowering water levels in four glacial lakes in the Himalayas. The project, estimated to cost ₹474 crore, aims to reduce the threat of flooding in Nepal and India and is expected to be completed by 2033.

Four glacial lakes identified for the project

The Nepalese government has selected Thulagi Lake in Manang district, Lower Barun and Hongu-2 lakes in Sankhuwasabha, and Lumding Lake in Solukhumbu. Located at altitudes between 4,050 and 5,483 metres, these lakes pose a potential risk if their water levels rise or their natural barriers fail.

Under the plan, the water level of Hongu-2 Lake will be lowered by one metre, while those of Thulagi, Lower Barun and Lumding lakes will each be reduced by three metres.

Water from three of these lakes flows into the Koshi and Gandaki river systems, which pass through Bihar. The project could help protect settlements, farmland, roads and other infrastructure from flood damage.

How will the water levels be reduced?

The project will involve constructing drainage canals along the lakes and installing gates to regulate water flow. Water will be released gradually into the rivers, without using explosives.

Construction will rely on workers and technical methods designed to minimise risks during the process.

According to Dr Bhattarai, the water levels could be lowered within three years if work proceeds without interruption. However, the lakes are situated in high-altitude regions where harsh weather restricts construction to five or six months annually. This has led authorities to set 2033 as the project's completion target.

He said the project would not eliminate the flood risk entirely but would prioritise the four lakes considered capable of causing the greatest damage if they burst.

47 glacial lakes in India, Nepal and China pose a threat

The devastating flooding in Nepal's Bhotekoshi River in August renewed concerns about the dangers posed by glacial lakes in the Himalayan region.

A 2020 report by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development identified 47 glacial lakes across India, Nepal and China as being at high risk. Of these, 21 are in Nepal, 25 in China and one in India.

The report found that water from 42 of these lakes flows into the Koshi River system, including 24 lakes in China and 18 in Nepal. The Koshi enters Bihar from Nepal, meaning a glacial lake outburst could threaten communities in both countries.

A picture of the flood that struck on 26 August. The floodwaters arrived so rapidly that people did not even have time to compose themselves and reach a safe place.

Green Climate Fund to contribute ₹343 crore

The project has a total estimated cost of ₹474 crore, with the Green Climate Fund providing ₹343 crore. The fund was established under the United Nations climate framework.

The Nepalese government will contribute ₹107 crore, while the UNDP will provide ₹20 crore. An additional ₹3 crore is expected from the private sector.

The project is expected to benefit more than 38 lakh people in Nepal and could reduce potential flood-related economic losses by up to ₹212 crore.
